Documento(s) de cenário:
--- Project Scenario 9.pdf ---
Core Financial System (FFMIA Compliance Initiative)
So here's where we are. We've got this thing hanging over us with FFMIA — basically the
law says our financial management system has to substantially comply with a whole set of
federal requirements, and right now nobody's totally confident we'd pass if someone came
in and checked us against that standard tomorrow. So the real driver here isn't "let's build
something cool," it's "we need a system that can actually stand up when auditors or the
inspector general come knocking and ask us to prove our books are clean and under
control."
The core of it is the general ledger — that's really the heart of everything, every other piece
hangs off of it. We need to be able to classify and track transactions properly: by fund, by
program, by organization, by project, by cost center, all that breakdown, because that's
how budget and program managers actually slice and dice the data later. On top of that we
need solid control over funds so we never end up obligating or spending more than what
was actually appropriated to us, that's a hard line, not negotiable. Then there's the
payment side — vendors, payees, getting money out the door correctly and being able to
track and confirm that a payment actually went where it should. And on the flip side, we
need to handle money coming in too, recording what's owed to the agency and following
up when people don't pay.
Cost management is something we want in there as well, even if it's not glamorous —
being able to actually measure what programs cost and what they're producing matters a
lot for budget conversations down the line. And reporting ties the whole thing together:
management needs timely numbers to make decisions, and we have to be able to produce
the formal financial statements and reports that get sent up the chain, to oversight bodies
and eventually made public.
Who's going to be touching this thing day to day: financial systems analysts, accountants,
program managers, the people who actually run agency operations and need to pull
numbers, and then auditors who'll come in periodically and poke at everything. So usability
for non-technical finance folks matters, this can't be something only an IT person can
operate.
On the technical side we do care about things like making sure it can handle the workload
without falling over, that it talks properly with other systems we already have instead of
becoming an island, that there's a real audit trail and security around who can touch what,
and decent web access so people aren't stuck only using it from one terminal somewhere.
That said, some of the fancier stuff — bells and whistles that are "nice to have" rather than
something a law or regulation forces on us — that's not where we want to spend our first
round of effort. If it's not mandatory and it's not clearly going to make somebody's job
dramatically easier, it can wait, we shouldn't be chasing every optional feature in the first
pass. The priority is getting the mandatory groundwork solid first.

Sistema: Core Financial System (FFMIA Compliance Initiative)

Resumo executivo: The Core Financial System supports an agency's FFMIA compliance initiative by providing controlled general-ledger, funds, payment, receivables, cost-management, reporting, auditability, and web-access capabilities. It enables finance and program stakeholders to maintain accountable financial records, prevent spending beyond appropriations, and provide evidence for audit and oversight activities.

Escopo: The system manages agency financial transactions, controls, reporting, and audit evidence through a web-accessible financial management solution.
  Em escopo: General-ledger transaction recording and classification
  Em escopo: Funds control against appropriations
  Em escopo: Vendor, payee, and payment management
  Em escopo: Accounts-receivable recording and delinquency identification
  Em escopo: Program cost and output measurement
  Em escopo: Management reports and formal financial statements
  Em escopo: Audit trail, role-based access control, web access, and integration with existing systems
  Fora de escopo: Optional features not required by law, regulation, or a demonstrated material improvement to user work — deferred from the first implementation
  Fora de escopo: Specific interfaces, protocols, and data mappings for external systems — [TBD] because the connected systems were not identified
  Premissa: PA-01: Authorized finance, program, operations, and audit personnel will be identified and assigned roles before production use. [INFERRED]
  Premissa: PA-02: Appropriation, organizational, fund, program, project, and cost-center reference data will be available for loading into the system. [INFERRED]
  Premissa: PA-03: The agency will define the FFMIA compliance criteria and report formats applicable to its operations. [TBD]
  Restrição: REST-01 (Regulatory): The system must substantially comply with applicable FFMIA federal financial-management requirements.
  Restrição: REST-02 (Operational): The first implementation must prioritize mandatory compliance capabilities over optional features.
  Restrição: REST-03 (Technical): The system must be accessible through a web interface and interoperate with existing agency systems.

Stakeholders:
  STK-01 - Financial systems analyst (Usuário primário): Maintain financial-system configuration, review transaction processing, and support compliance evidence.
  STK-02 - Accountant (Usuário primário): Record and classify ledger transactions, manage payments and receivables, and prepare financial statements.
  STK-03 - Program manager (Usuário primário): Analyze program costs, outputs, funds, and management reports.
  STK-04 - Agency operations personnel (Usuário secundário): Retrieve operational financial information for agency activities.
  STK-05 - Auditor / Inspector General (Stakeholder externo): Examine financial records, access controls, audit trails, and compliance evidence.
  STK-06 - Oversight body (Stakeholder externo): Receive formal financial reports and statements.
  STK-07 - Vendor or payee (Stakeholder externo): Receive payments directed to the correct payee.

Regras de negócio:
  RN-001 - FFMIA substantial compliance: Agency financial management must substantially comply with applicable FFMIA federal requirements.
  RN-002 - Transaction classification: Each financial transaction must be classified by fund, program, organization, project, and cost center.
  RN-003 - Appropriation limit: Obligations and expenditures must not exceed the amount appropriated to the agency.
  RN-004 - Payment confirmation: A payment must be traceable to its intended vendor or payee and its delivery status.
  RN-005 - Receivable follow-up: Amounts owed to the agency must be recorded and receivables past their due date must be subject to follow-up.
  RN-006 - Financial reporting: Formal financial statements and reports must be produced for management, oversight, and public reporting purposes.

Requisitos funcionais:
  RF-001 - Record general-ledger entry: The system shall record a general-ledger entry with transaction date, amount, account, and transaction identifier. [Must have]
  RF-002 - Classify transaction: The system shall assign fund, program, organization, project, and cost-center classifications to each financial transaction. [Must have]
  RF-003 - Calculate available appropriation: The system shall calculate the available appropriation for a selected fund before an obligation or expenditure is recorded. [Must have]
  RF-004 - Block excess obligation or expenditure: The system shall reject an obligation or expenditure whose amount exceeds the available appropriation. [Must have]
  RF-005 - Register payee: The system shall register vendor or payee identification data for a payment. [Must have]
  RF-006 - Record payment: The system shall record a payment with its payee, amount, date, and payment identifier. [Must have]
  RF-007 - Track payment status: The system shall store the delivery status for each recorded payment. [Must have]
  RF-008 - Record receivable: The system shall record an amount owed to the agency with debtor, amount, due date, and receivable identifier. [Must have]
  RF-009 - Identify delinquent receivable: The system shall identify a receivable as delinquent when its due date has passed and its outstanding balance is greater than zero. [Must have]
  RF-010 - Record program cost: The system shall record a cost against a program. [Must have]
  RF-011 - Record program output: The system shall record an output measure against a program. [Must have]
  RF-012 - Generate management report: The system shall generate a management financial report filtered by fund, program, organization, project, or cost center. [Must have]
  RF-013 - Generate formal financial statement: The system shall generate a formal financial statement using agency-approved reporting formats. [TBD] [Must have]
  RF-014 - Record audit event: The system shall record the user, timestamp, action, and affected record identifier for each create, update, delete, approval, and access-control event. [Must have]
  RF-015 - Enforce role authorization: The system shall restrict each function to users assigned an authorized role. [Must have]
  RF-016 - Provide web access: The system shall provide authorized users access to its functions through a web browser. [Must have]
  RF-017 - Exchange data with existing systems: The system shall exchange financial data with each agency system identified for integration. [TBD] [Must have]

Requisitos não funcionais:
  RNF-001 (Performance Efficiency) - The system shall complete general-ledger transaction submission within 2 seconds at the 95th percentile under 200 concurrent users. [TBD] | Métrica: 95% of submissions complete in 2 seconds or less with 200 concurrent users.
  RNF-002 (Reliability) - The system shall maintain at least 99.5% monthly availability, excluding announced maintenance windows. [TBD] | Métrica: Maximum unplanned downtime of 3.6 hours per 30-day month.
  RNF-003 (Security) - The system shall deny 100% of authorization-test requests for functions not assigned to the requesting user's role. | Métrica: 0 unauthorized function executions in the role-authorization test suite.
  RNF-004 (Security) - The system shall retain audit records for 100% of tested create, update, delete, approval, and access-control events. | Métrica: 100% of 500 sampled events have user, timestamp, action, and affected-record identifier.
  RNF-005 (Interaction Capability) - The system shall enable at least 80% of five non-technical finance participants to record a classified general-ledger entry within 10 minutes after a standardized 15-minute orientation. [TBD] | Métrica: At least 4 of 5 participants complete the task without facilitator intervention.
  RNF-006 (Compatibility) - The system shall process at least 99% of valid integration messages from identified agency systems without manual re-entry. [TBD] | Métrica: At least 990 of 1,000 valid test messages are processed successfully.
  RNF-007 (Functional Suitability) - The system shall satisfy 100% of agency-approved applicable FFMIA compliance test cases. [TBD] | Métrica: 100% pass rate for the approved applicable FFMIA test suite.

Casos de uso:
  UC-001 - Record classified general-ledger entry | Ator: Accountant
    1. The accountant starts a new general-ledger entry.
    2. The system displays entry fields and classification fields.
    3. The accountant enters the transaction data and classifications.
    4. The system validates required data.
    5. The system records the entry and its audit event.
  UC-002 - Control obligation against appropriation | Ator: Accountant
    1. The accountant enters an obligation or expenditure amount and fund.
    2. The system calculates the available appropriation.
    3. The system compares the requested amount with the available appropriation.
    4. The system records the transaction when the requested amount does not exceed the available appropriation.
  UC-003 - Record and confirm payment | Ator: Accountant
    1. The accountant selects a registered payee.
    2. The accountant enters the payment amount and date.
    3. The system records the payment.
    4. The system stores the payment delivery status.
    5. The system records the audit event.
  UC-004 - Identify delinquent receivable | Ator: Accountant
    1. The accountant requests the receivables review.
    2. The system evaluates each receivable due date and outstanding balance.
    3. The system marks each receivable past due with a balance greater than zero as delinquent.
    4. The system displays the delinquent receivables.
  UC-005 - Generate management financial report | Ator: Program manager
    1. The program manager selects a reporting dimension and filter value.
    2. The system validates the user's reporting access.
    3. The system retrieves matching financial data.
    4. The system generates the report.
  UC-006 - Review audit trail | Ator: Auditor / Inspector General
    1. The auditor enters audit-trail search criteria.
    2. The system validates audit-review authorization.
    3. The system retrieves matching audit records.
    4. The system displays the user, timestamp, action, and affected-record identifier for each record.

Critérios de aceite:
  CA-001 - Dado an authorized accountant has entered a transaction date, amount, account, and transaction identifier, quando the accountant submits the general-ledger entry, então the system stores one entry with the submitted values and returns a unique entry identifier
  CA-002 - Dado an authorized accountant is creating a financial transaction, quando the accountant submits fund, program, organization, project, and cost-center values, então the system stores the five submitted classifications on the transaction
  CA-003 - Dado a fund has an appropriation of 1000.00 and recorded obligations and expenditures totaling 700.00, quando an accountant selects the fund for a new transaction, então the system displays an available appropriation of 300.00
  CA-004 - Dado a fund has an available appropriation of 300.00, quando an accountant submits an obligation for 300.01, então the system rejects the transaction, records no obligation, and displays the available appropriation of 300.00
  CA-005 - Dado an authorized accountant has entered a vendor or payee identification value, quando the accountant submits the payee record, então the system stores one payee record and returns a unique payee identifier
  CA-006 - Dado a payee is registered, quando an authorized accountant submits a payment with payee, amount, date, and payment identifier, então the system stores one payment record with the submitted values
  CA-007 - Dado a payment is recorded, quando the system receives a delivery status of 'Delivered', então the system stores 'Delivered' as the payment delivery status for that payment identifier
  CA-008 - Dado an authorized accountant has entered a debtor, amount, due date, and receivable identifier, quando the accountant submits the receivable, então the system stores one receivable with the submitted values
  CA-009 - Dado a receivable has a due date before the current date and an outstanding balance of 1.00, quando the receivables review is executed, então the system sets the receivable status to 'Delinquent'
  CA-010 - Dado an authorized program manager selects a program, quando the manager submits a cost amount, então the system stores the cost amount against the selected program
  CA-011 - Dado an authorized program manager selects a program, quando the manager submits an output measure, então the system stores the output measure against the selected program
  CA-012 - Dado a program manager is authorized to view data for fund F-01, quando the manager generates a report filtered by fund F-01, então the system generates a report containing only records classified with fund F-01
  CA-013 - Dado an accountant selects an agency-approved reporting format, quando the accountant requests a formal financial statement, então the system generates one statement in the selected approved format
  CA-014 - Dado an authorized user updates a financial record, quando the update is committed, então the system stores one audit record containing the user, timestamp, 'Update' action, and affected-record identifier
  CA-015 - Dado a user is not assigned the role required to approve a financial action, quando the user requests the approval function, então the system denies the function and creates no approval record
  CA-016 - Dado an authorized user opens a supported web browser, quando the user navigates to the system web address and authenticates, então the system displays the user's authorized functions in the browser
  CA-017 - Dado an identified agency system sends a valid financial-data message, quando the Core Financial System receives the message through the approved integration, então the system processes the message once and returns a successful processing status

Glossário:
  FFMIA: Federal Financial Management Improvement Act; the compliance driver identified for this initiative.
  General ledger: The central accounting record in which financial transactions are recorded.
  Appropriation: An amount authorized for agency use that limits obligations and expenditures.
  Obligation: A commitment of appropriated funds that reduces the amount available for future use.
  Payee: The vendor or other recipient designated to receive a payment.
  Receivable: An amount owed to the agency.
  Cost center: An organizational classification used to attribute and analyze costs.
  Audit trail: A chronological record of system events that identifies who performed an action, when it occurred, and which record was affected.

Base: ISO/IEC/IEEE 29148:2018 §9.6 · IEEE 830-1998 §3 · Sommerville (2016, cap. 4)
O Documento de Especificação de Requisitos de Software (SRS) é o contrato técnico que descreve o 
que o sistema deve fazer e sob quais condições de qualidade. Ele serve de referência para 
desenvolvedores, testadores, gerentes e clientes durante todo o ciclo de vida do projeto.
1.1 Artefatos Obrigatórios e sua Ordem
Um SRS completo e formal deve conter os seguintes artefatos, nesta ordem:
• ESCOPO: Define o que está DENTRO e FORA do projeto. Evita scope creep.
• STAKEHOLDERS: Lista todos os envolvidos: quem usa, quem financia, quem é afetado.
• PREMISSAS E RESTRIÇÕES: Fatos assumidos como verdadeiros e limites impostos ao projeto.
• REGRAS DE NEGÓCIO (RN): Políticas, fórmulas e condições de negócio que existem independentemente 
do software.
• REQUISITOS FUNCIONAIS (RF): O que o sistema DEVE FAZER — comportamentos, serviços, respostas a 
entradas.
• REQUISITOS NÃO FUNCIONAIS (RNF): Como o sistema deve SER — atributos de qualidade 
quantificáveis.
• HISTÓRIAS DE USUÁRIO (HU): Necessidades na perspectiva do usuário: Como [perfil], quero [ação], para
[benefício].
• CASOS DE USO (UC): Interações detalhadas ator-sistema com fluxo principal, alternativo e exceções.
• CRITÉRIOS DE ACEITE (CA): Condições testáveis em formato BDD (Dado/Quando/Então) que definem 
quando o requisito está concluído.
• GLOSSÁRIO: Termos do domínio com definição precisa para eliminar ambiguidades.
1.2 Como os Artefatos se Interconectam
Os artefatos formam uma cadeia de rastreabilidade. Cada RF deve ter origem em um STK 
(stakeholder) ou RN. Cada HU deve ter pelo menos um RF associado. Cada RF e HU devem ter pelo menos um CA. Esta rastreabilidade garante que nada seja implementado sem justificativa de 
negócio e que tudo que foi prometido seja testável.
Cadeia de rastreabilidade mínima:
STK → (RN →) RF → HU → CA

When old requirements don’t exist
Most older systems do not have documented—let alone accurate—requirements. In the absence of 
reliable documentation, teams might reverse-engineer an understanding of what the system does 
from the user interfaces, code, and database. We think of this as “software archaeology.” To maximize 
the benefit from reverse engineering, the archaeology expedition should record what it learns in 
the form of requirements and design descriptions. Accumulating accurate information about certain 
portions of the current system positions the team to enhance a system with low risk, to replace a 
system without missing critical functionality, and to perform future enhancements efficiently. It halts 
the knowledge drain, so future maintainers better understand the changes that were just made.
If updating the requirements is overly burdensome, it will fall by the wayside as busy people rush 
on to the next change request. Obsolete requirements aren’t helpful for future enhancements. There’s 
a widespread fear in the software industry that writing documentation will consume too much time; 
the knee-jerk reaction is to neglect all opportunities to update requirements documentation. But 
what’s the cost if you don’t update the requirements and a future maintainer (perhaps you!) has to 
regenerate that information? The answer to this question will let you make a thoughtful business 
decision concerning whether to revise the requirements documentation when you change or 
re-create the software.
When the team performs additional enhancements and maintenance over time, it can extend 
these fractional knowledge representations, steadily improving the system documentation. The 
incremental cost of recording this newly found knowledge is small compared with the cost of 
someone having to rediscover it later on. Implementing enhancements almost always necessitates 
further requirements development, so add those new requirements to an existing requirements 
repository, if there is one. If you’re replacing an old system, you have an opportunity to document 
the requirements for the new one and to keep the requirements up to date with what you learn 
throughout the project. Try to leave the requirements in better shape than you found them.
Which requirements should you specify?
It’s not always worth taking the time to generate a complete set of requirements for an entire 
production system. Many options lie between the two extremes of continuing forever with no 
requirements documentation and reconstructing a perfect requirements set. Knowing why you’d like 
to have written requirements available lets you judge whether the cost of rebuilding all—or even 
part—of the specification is a sound investment.

Expected challenges
The presence of an existing system leads to common challenges that both enhancement and 
replacement projects will face, including the following:
■ The changes made could degrade the performance to which users are accustomed.
■ Little or no requirements documentation might be available for the existing system.
■ Users who are familiar with how the system works today might not like the changes they are 
about to encounter.
■ You might unknowingly break or omit functionality that is vital to some stakeholder group.
■ Stakeholders might take this opportunity to request new functionality that seems like a good 
idea but isn’t really needed to meet the business objectives.
Even if there is existing documentation, it might not prove useful. For enhancement projects, 
the documentation might not be up to date. If the documentation doesn’t match the existing 
application’s reality, it is of limited use. For replacement systems, you also need to be wary of carrying 
forward all of the requirements, because some of the old functionality probably should not be 
migrated.
One of the major issues in replacement projects is validating that the reasons for the replacement 
are sound. There need to be justifiable business objectives for the change. When existing systems 
are being completely replaced, organizational processes might also have to change, which makes it 
harder for people to accept a new system. The change in business processes, change in the software 
system, and learning curve of a new system can disrupt current operations.

If you’re replacing an old system, you have an opportunity to document 
the requirements for the new one and to keep the requirements up to date with what you learn 
throughout the project. Try to leave the requirements in better shape than you found them.
Which requirements should you specify?
It’s not always worth taking the time to generate a complete set of requirements for an entire 
production system. Many options lie between the two extremes of continuing forever with no 
requirements documentation and reconstructing a perfect requirements set. Knowing why you’d like 
to have written requirements available lets you judge whether the cost of rebuilding all—or even 
part—of the specification is a sound investment.

Rarely do you need to document the entire existing system. Focus detailed requirements efforts 
on the changes needed to meet the business objectives. If you’re replacing a system, start by 
documenting the areas prioritized as most important to achieve the business objectives or those that 
pose the highest implementation risk. Any new requirements identified during the gap analysis will 
need to be specified at the same level of precision and using the same techniques as you would for a 
new system.
Level of detail
One of the biggest challenges is determining the appropriate level of detail at which to document 
requirements gleaned from the existing system. For enhancements, defining requirements for the 
new functionality alone might be sufficient. However, you will usually benefit from documenting all of 
the functionality that closely relates to the enhancement, to ensure that the change fits in seamlessly 
(region B in Figure 21-2). You might want to create business processes, user requirements, and/or 
functional requirements for those related areas. For example, let’s say you are adding a discount code 
feature to an existing shopping cart function, but you don’t have any documented requirements for 
the shopping cart. You might be tempted to write just a single user story: “As a customer, I need to be 
able to enter a discount code so I can get the cheapest price for the product.” However, this user story 
alone lacks context, so consider capturing other user stories about shopping cart operations. That 
information could be valuable the next time you need to modify the shopping cart function.
I worked with one team that was just beginning to develop the requirements for version 2 of 
a major product with embedded software. They hadn’t done a good job on the requirements for 
version 1, which was currently being implemented. The lead BA wondered, “Is it worth going back 
to improve the SRS for version 1?” The company anticipated that this product line would be a major 
revenue generator for at least 10 years. They also planned to reuse some of the core requirements 
in several spin-off products. In this case, it made sense to improve the requirements documentation 
for version 1 because it was the foundation for all subsequent development work in this product line.

Os artefatos formam uma cadeia de rastreabilidade. Cada RF deve ter origem em um STK 
(stakeholder) ou RN. Cada HU deve ter pelo menos um RF associado. Cada RF e HU devem ter pelo menos um CA. Esta rastreabilidade garante que nada seja implementado sem justificativa de 
negócio e que tudo que foi prometido seja testável.

1.3 Princípios Fundamentais de Qualidade de Requisitos
Base: ISO/IEC/IEEE 29148:2018 §5.2 — Características do requisito individual
• Necessário: Existe uma necessidade real que o justifica. Sem o requisito, há uma lacuna de negócio.
• Não ambíguo: Tem uma única interpretação possível. Evitar: 'eficiente', 'fácil', 'rápido', 'amigável'.
• Verificável: Pode ser testado objetivamente com critério mensurável. 'Rápido' não é verificável; '< 2 s' é.
• Singular: Descreve uma única coisa. Nunca usar 'e' ou 'ou' para combinar dois comportamentos em um 
RF.
• Viável: Tecnicamente e financeiramente possível dentro das restrições do projeto.
• Rastreável: Tem origem (stakeholder ou RN) e destino (caso de teste) identificados.
• Completo: Contém todas as informações necessárias para implementação sem consultas adicionais.
• Consistente: Não conflita com nenhum outro requisito do documento.
• Priorizado: Tem um nível de prioridade definido (MoSCoW: Must/Should/Could/Won't).PARTE 2 — Padrões de Escrita por Artefato

Core Financial System (FFMIA Compliance Initiative)
So here's where we are. We've got this thing hanging over us with FFMIA — basically the
law says our financial management system has to substantially comply with a whole set of
federal requirements, and right now nobody's totally confident we'd pass if someone came
in and checked us against that standard tomorrow. So the real driver here isn't "let's build
something cool," it's "we need a system that can actually stand up when auditors or the
inspector general come knocking and ask us to prove our books are clean and under
control."
The core of it is the general ledger — that's really the heart of everything, every other piece
hangs off of it. We need to be able to classify and track transactions properly: by fund, by
program, by organization, by project, by cost center, all that breakdown, because that's
how budget and program managers actually slice and dice the data later. On top of that we
need solid control over funds so we never end up obligating or spending more than what
was actually appropriated to us, that's a hard line, not negotiable. Then there's the
payment side — vendors, payees, getting money out the door correctly and being able to
track and confirm that a payment actually went where it should. And on the flip side, we
need to handle money coming in too, recording what's owed to the agency and following
up when people don't pay.
Cost management is something we want in there as well, even if it's not glamorous —
being able to actually measure what programs cost and what they're producing matters a
lot for budget conversations down the line. And reporting ties the whole thing together:
management needs timely numbers to make decisions, and we have to be able to produce
the formal financial statements and reports that get sent up the chain, to oversight bodies
and eventually made public.
Who's going to be touching this thing day to day: financial systems analysts, accountants,
program managers, the people who actually run agency operations and need to pull
numbers, and then auditors who'll come in periodically and poke at everything. So usability
for non-technical finance folks matters, this can't be something only an IT person can
operate.
On the technical side we do care about things like making sure it can handle the workload
without falling over, that it talks properly with other systems we already have instead of
becoming an island, that there's a real audit trail and security around who can touch what,
and decent web access so people aren't stuck only using it from one terminal somewhere.
That said, some of the fancier stuff — bells and whistles that are "nice to have" rather than
something a law or regulation forces on us — that's not where we want to spend our first
round of effort. If it's not mandatory and it's not clearly going to make somebody's job
dramatically easier, it can wait, we shouldn't be chasing every optional feature in the first
pass. The priority is getting the mandatory groundwork solid first.

If developers build exactly what 
customers initially request, they’ll probably have to build it again because customers often don’t 
know what they really need. In addition, the BAs might not be talking to the right people or asking 
the right questions.
The features that users present as their “wants” don’t necessarily equate to the functionality they 
need to perform their tasks with the new product. To gain a more accurate view of user needs, the 
business analyst must collect a wide range of user input, analyze and clarify it, and specify just what 
needs to be built to let users do their jobs. The BA has the lead responsibility for recording the new 
system’s necessary capabilities and properties and for communicating that information to other 
stakeholders. This is an iterative process that takes time. If you don’t invest the time to achieve this 
shared understanding—this common vision of the intended product—the certain outcomes are 
rework, missed deadlines, cost overruns, and customer dissatisfaction.
User classes
People often talk about “the user” for a software system as though all users belong to a monolithic 
group with similar characteristics and needs. In reality, most products of any size appeal to a diversity 
of users with different expectations and goals. Rather than thinking of “the user” in singular, spend 
some time identifying the multiple user classes and their roles and privileges for your product.
Classifying users
Chapter 2 described many of the types of stakeholders that a project might have. As shown in 
Figure 6-1, a user class is a subset of the product’s users, which is a subset of the product’s customers, 
which is a subset of its stakeholders. An individual can belong to multiple user classes. For example, 
an application’s administrator might also interact with it as an ordinary user at times. A product’s 
users might differ—among other ways—in the following respects, and you can group users into a 
number of distinct user classes based on these sorts of differences:
■ Their access privilege or security levels (such as ordinary user, guest user, administrator)
■ The tasks they perform during their business operations
■ The features they use
■ The frequency with which they use the product
■ Their application domain experience and computer systems expertise
■ The platforms they will be using (desktop PCs, laptop PCs, tablets, smartphones, specialized 
devices)CHAPTER 6 Finding the voice of the user 103
■ Their native language
■ Whether they will interact with the system directly or indirectly
FIGURE 6-1 A hierarchy of stakeholders, customers, users, and user classes.
It’s tempting to group users into classes based on their geographical location or the kind of 
company they work in. One company that creates software used in the banking industry initially 
considered distinguishing users based on whether they worked in a large commercial bank, a small 
commercial bank, a savings and loan institution, or a credit union. These distinctions really represent 
different market segments, though, not different user classes.
A better way to identify user classes is to think about the tasks that various users will perform with 
the system. All of those types of financial institutions will have tellers, employees who process loan 
applications, business bankers, and so forth. The individuals who perform such activities—whether 
they are job titles or simply roles—will have similar functional needs for the system across all of the 
financial institutions. Tellers all have to do more or less the same things, business bankers do more or 
less the same things, and so on. More logical user class names for a banking system therefore might 
include teller, loan officer, business banker, and branch manager. You might discover additional user 
classes by thinking of possible use cases, user stories, and process flows and who might perform them.

Enhancement and replacement 
projects
Most of this book describes requirements development as though you are beginning a new software 
or system development project, sometimes called a green-field project. However, many organizations 
devote much of their effort to enhancing or replacing existing information systems or building 
new releases of established commercial products. Most of the practices described in this book are 
appropriate for enhancement and replacement projects. This chapter provides specific suggestions as 
to which practices are most relevant and how to use them.
An enhancement project is one in which new capabilities are added to an existing system. 
Enhancement projects might also involve correcting defects, adding new reports, and modifying 
functionality to comply with revised business rules or needs.
A replacement (or reengineering) project replaces an existing application with a new custom-built 
system, a commercial off-the-shelf (COTS) system, or a hybrid of those. Replacement projects are 
most commonly implemented to improve performance, cut costs (such as maintenance costs or 
license fees), take advantage of modern technologies, or meet regulatory requirements. If your 
replacement project will involve a COTS solution, the guidance presented in Chapter 22, “Packaged 
solution projects,” will also be helpful.
Replacement and enhancement projects face some particular requirements issues. The original 
developers who held all the critical information in their heads might be long gone. It’s tempting to 
claim that a small enhancement doesn’t warrant writing any requirements. Developers might believe 
that they don’t need detailed requirements if they are replacing an existing system’s functionality. 
The approaches described in this chapter can help you to deal with the challenges of enhancing or 
replacing an existing system to improve its ability to meet the organization’s current business needs.
The case of the missing spec
The requirements specification for the next release of a mature system often says, essentially, 
“The new system should do everything the old system does, except add these new features 
and fix those bugs.” A business analyst once received just such a specification for version 5 of 
a major product. To find out exactly what the current release did, she looked at the SRS for 
version 4. Unfortunately, it also said, in essence, “Version 4 should do everything that version 3 
does, except add these new features and fix those bugs.” She followed the trail back, but every

Prioritizing by using business objectives
Enhancement projects are undertaken to add new capabilities to an existing application. It’s easy 
to get caught up in the excitement and start adding unnecessary capabilities. To combat this risk 
of gold-plating, trace requirements back to business objectives to ensure that the new features are 
needed and to select the highest-impact features to implement first. You also might need to prioritize 
enhancement requests against the correction of defects that had been reported against the old 
system.
Also be wary of letting unnecessary new functionality slip into replacement projects. The main 
focus of replacement projects is to migrate existing functionality. However, customers might imagine 
that if you are developing a new system anyway, it is easy to add lots of new capabilities right away. 
Many replacement projects have collapsed because of the weight of uncontrolled scope growth. 
You’re usually better off building a stable first release and adding more features through subsequent 
enhancement projects, provided the first release allows users to do their jobs.
Replacement projects often originate when stakeholders want to add functionality to an existing 
system that is too inflexible to support the growth or has technology limitations. However, there needs 
to be a clear business objective to justify implementing an expensive new system (Devine 2008). Use 
the anticipated cost savings from a new system (such as through reduced maintenance of an old, 
clunky system) plus the value of the new desired functionality to justify a system replacement project.
Also look for existing functionality that doesn’t need to be retained in a replacement system. Don’t 
replicate the existing system’s shortcomings or miss an opportunity to update a system to suit new 
business needs and processes. For example, the BA might ask users, “Do you use <a particular menu 
option>?” If you consistently hear “I never do that,” then maybe it isn’t needed in the replacement 
system. Look for usage data that shows what screens, functions, or data entities are rarely accessed 
in the current system. Even the existing functionality has to map to current and anticipated business 
objectives to warrant re-implementing it in the new system.
Trap Don’t let stakeholders get away with saying “I have it today, so I need it in the new 
system” as a default method of justifying requirements.
Mind the gap
A gap analysis is a comparison of functionality between an existing system and a desired new system. 
A gap analysis can be expressed in different ways, including use cases, user stories, or features. When 
enhancing an existing system, perform a gap analysis to make sure you understand why it isn’t 
currently meeting your business objectives.
Gap analysis for a replacement project entails understanding existing functionality and discovering 
the desired new functionality (see Figure 21-1). Identify user requirements for the existing system that 
stakeholders want to have re-implemented in the new system. Also, elicit new user requirements that 
the existing system does not address. Consider any change requests that were never implemented CHAPTER 21 Enhancement and replacement projects 397
in the existing system. Prioritize the existing user requirements and the new ones together. Prioritize 
closing the gaps using business objectives as described in the previous section or the other

Existing systems set user expectations for performance and throughput. Stakeholders almost

2 BACKGROUND
This section briefly describes ISO 29148 emphasizing the suggested process items with which 
the axes of analysis are established and presents the relevant aspects of RE and the UC 
paradigm.
2.1 ISO/IEC/IEEE 29148
ISO 29148 is a systems and software engineering standard that specifies the required 
processes to determine the product requirements (including services) of systems and software 
throughout the life cycle (ISO/IEC/IEEE, 2018), (IEEE-CS, 2014). ISO 29148 is aligned with 
ISO/IEC/IEEE 12207 standard for software life cycle processes and ISO/IEC/IEEE 15288 
standard for system life cycle processes (IEEE-CS, 2014). ISO 29148, in its first edition (2011), 
replaced the IEEE 830-1998, IEEE 1233-1998 and IEEE 1362-1998 standards, also related to 
requirements engineering (IEEE SA, 2011), becoming the main standard in RE by providing a 
model adaptable to different organizations (Selvyanti & Bandung, 2017). In 2018, the second 
edition was published, due to the need to adopt a framework oriented towards a more detailed C2-4
technical approach (Ward et al., 2018), and in Boyarchuk et al. (2020) the importance of having 
a structured process in RE to build a good software product is highlighted.
ISO 29148 establishes (ISO/IEC/IEEE, 2018): (i) a set of 3 main processes that are iteratively 
and recursively applied in the system and software life cycle (see Fig. 1); (ii) a set of 2 related 
technical processes; (iii) each main process is composed of activities with established 
objectives to achieve a correct identification and good description of requirements; (iv) a set of 4 
types of documents for requirements specification at business, stakeholder, system and 
software levels; (v) the concept of operations and System operational concept; and, (vi) 
guidelines to manage the evolution of requirements.
2.2 User-Centered Software Requirements
The user-centered software development approach (UCD), was stablished as a response to 
existing software development schemes, which in practical terms can be noted, were focused 
on the technical aspect of the software and associated hardware (De Bellis & Haapala, 1995), 
(Norman & Draper, 1987). The UCD gained some relevance with the publication of ISO 
13407:1999 Human-centred Design Processes for Interactive Systems (Juárez-Ramírez, 2017)
and after that, when the stakeholders are included into ISO 9241-210:2010 Ergonomics of 
human-system interaction - Part 210: Human-centred Design for Interactive Systems (Vidal et 
al., 2012). Finally, the latest edition of the ISO 9241-210 standard is, recently, from 2019 (IEEE 
SA, 2011). In short, as pointed out by several authors (Juárez-Ramírez, 2017), (Forbrig, 2016), 
(Nieva et al., 2016), (Wanderley et al., 2014), and the ISO 13407 standard itself (ISO, 2019), 
RE should allow to reach an understanding of the needs, attitudes, motivations and behaviors of 
users that are the basis for achieving successful products and services, with a wide margin of 
end-user satisfaction.

casos_de_uso.pre_condicao: The accountant is authenticated and authorized to record general-ledger entries.
casos_de_uso.pos_condicao_sucesso: A general-ledger entry is recorded with all required classifications and an audit record.
fluxo_principal: 1. The accountant starts a new general-ledger entry.
2. The system displays entry fields and classification fields.
3. The accountant enters the transaction data and classifications.
4. The system validates required data.
5. The system records the entry and its audit event.
fluxos_alternativos: 4a. A required classification is absent → the system identifies the absent field; returns to step 3.
fluxos_excecao: 4b. The user is not authorized → the system denies the action and records the access-control event (ref. RF-015, RF-014).

casos_de_uso.pre_condicao: The accountant is authenticated and an appropriation is available for the selected fund.
casos_de_uso.pos_condicao_sucesso: The obligation or expenditure is recorded without exceeding the available appropriation.
casos_de_uso.pos_condicao_falha: No obligation or expenditure exceeding the available appropriation is recorded.
fluxo_principal: 1. The accountant enters an obligation or expenditure amount and fund.
2. The system calculates the available appropriation.
3. The system compares the requested amount with the available appropriation.
4. The system records the transaction when the requested amount does not exceed the available appropriation.
fluxos_alternativos: 3a. The requested amount equals the available appropriation → the system records the transaction and sets the remaining amount to zero.
fluxos_excecao: 3b. The requested amount exceeds the available appropriation → the system rejects the transaction and displays the remaining available amount (ref. RN-003, RF-004).

casos_de_uso.pre_condicao: The accountant is authenticated and the payee is registered.
casos_de_uso.pos_condicao_sucesso: The payment and its delivery status are recorded for the selected payee.
fluxo_principal: 1. The accountant selects a registered payee.
2. The accountant enters the payment amount and date.
3. The system records the payment.
4. The system stores the payment delivery status.
5. The system records the audit event.
fluxos_alternativos: 4a. Delivery status is pending → the system stores the status as 'Pending confirmation'.
fluxos_excecao: 1b. The payee is not registered → the system prevents payment recording and requests payee registration (ref. RF-005).

casos_de_uso.pre_condicao: A receivable with a due date and outstanding balance is recorded.
casos_de_uso.pos_condicao_sucesso: Each overdue receivable with an outstanding balance is identified as delinquent.
casos_de_uso.pos_condicao_falha: Receivables not meeting the delinquency condition remain unchanged.
fluxo_principal: 1. The accountant requests the receivables review.
2. The system evaluates each receivable due date and outstanding balance.
3. The system marks each receivable past due with a balance greater than zero as delinquent.
4. The system displays the delinquent receivables.
fluxos_alternativos: 2a. The due date has not passed → the system retains the current receivable status.
fluxos_excecao: 2b. A receivable has no due date → the system excludes it from delinquency identification and records a data-validation exception (ref. RN-005, RF-008).

casos_de_uso.pre_condicao: The program manager is authenticated and authorized to access the requested financial data.
casos_de_uso.pos_condicao_sucesso: A report filtered by the selected dimension is generated.
fluxo_principal: 1. The program manager selects a reporting dimension and filter value.
2. The system validates the user's reporting access.
3. The system retrieves matching financial data.
4. The system generates the report.
fluxos_alternativos: 3a. No matching data exists → the system generates a report showing zero matching records.
fluxos_excecao: 2b. The program manager lacks access to the selected data → the system denies report generation and records the event (ref. RF-015, RF-014).

casos_de_uso.pre_condicao: The auditor is authenticated and assigned audit-review access.
casos_de_uso.pos_condicao_sucesso: The auditor views matching audit records.
casos_de_uso.pos_condicao_falha: No audit records are disclosed to an unauthorized user.
fluxo_principal: 1. The auditor enters audit-trail search criteria.
2. The system validates audit-review authorization.
3. The system retrieves matching audit records.
4. The system displays the user, timestamp, action, and affected-record identifier for each record.
fluxos_alternativos: 3a. No audit records match the criteria → the system displays zero matching records.
fluxos_excecao: 2b. Authorization fails → the system denies access and records the access-control event (ref. RF-015, RF-014).

historias_de_usuario.descricao: As a financial systems analyst, I want to classify and track transactions by fund, program, organization, project, and cost center, so that program and budget managers can analyze the data.
As an accountant, I want the system to prevent obligations or spending beyond the appropriated amount, so that the agency stays within its funding limits.
As an accounts-payable owner, I want to process payments to vendors/payees and confirm they reached the correct destination, so that disbursements are accurate and traceable.
As an accounts-receivable owner, I want to record amounts owed to the agency and chase overdue payments, so that outstanding amounts are collected.
As a program manager, I want to see cost management data (what a program costs and produces), so that I can support budget decisions.
As agency management, I want formal financial statements and reports, so that I can report to oversight bodies and, eventually, the public.
As an auditor, I want to review a real audit trail and the system's access security controls, so that I can verify compliance during periodic reviews.
As agency operations staff, I want to access the system over the web from multiple locations, so that I'm not restricted to a single terminal.

casos_de_uso.descricao: Record and classify transaction — a user records a financial transaction in the general ledger, classified by fund, program, organization, project, and cost center.
Process vendor payment — the system processes a payment to a vendor/payee and confirms it reached the correct destination, respecting the funds control limit.
Track receivable — the system records an amount owed to the agency and flags it for follow-up when payment is not made.
Generate financial report — a user generates formal financial statements/reports for management, oversight bodies, or public release.
Audit system access — an auditor reviews the system's audit trail and access controls.

criterios_de_aceite.descricao: Given a transaction that would exceed the funds appropriated for its fund/program, when it is submitted, then the system prevents the obligation/expenditure from being recorded.
Given a payment issued to a vendor/payee, when the payment is processed, then the system tracks and confirms that it reached the correct destination.
Given a receivable with an overdue payment, when the due date passes without payment, then the system flags the case for follow-up.
Given a request for a formal financial statement, when it is generated, then the result is suitable for submission to management and to oversight bodies.
Given a user accessing the system, when any action is performed, then the system records it in an audit trail that identifies who did what.
